added_provisions.reason: The answer requires execution before two witnesses, but the corpus text of Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2(1)(a) says only 'the witnesses' and is in any event a post-2022 text. Rule (8) of Notaries Ordinance s.31 states the number and is untouched by the 2011, 2022 and 2024 amendment Acts.

The map recorded stamp duty as a corpus gap and rested the step on Notaries Ordinance rule (6), whose matter-date wording is unresolved. Section 22(2) of the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 is in the corpus and puts a direct duty on the attesting notary that does not depend on the rate.

Needed to show that s.22(2) of the 1982 Act still applies to a deed of transfer at the matter date: s.13 of Act No. 12 of 2006 excepts instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property from the displacement of the 1982 Act.
Gives the execution formality (executant and witnesses signing in the notary's presence and in one another's presence) a source that was in force in October 2020, which PROV-M062-007 cannot be.

question_decisions.note: The authority requirement is confirmed: every step in the answer comes from a statutory duty or restriction in the corpus and no case law or Roman-Dutch doctrine is cited or needed. The question is downgraded because two indispensable provisions are unresolved on temporal grounds: the 'tea estate' extent threshold in Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act s.25 (the answer states 'one hundred acres', a figure the corpus itself records as superseded by Act No. 20 of 2005 s.10(c)), and Prevention of Frauds Ordinance s.2, held only in its post-2022 form. Four provisions were added, the hop count of 4 was checked against the ceiling chain (s.66 to s.3(1)(b) to s.8 to s.5(1)) and left unchanged, and the arithmetic in the application limb (60 per cent of twenty acres is twelve, plus eighteen is thirty, below fifty) checks out.

disagreements.researcher_position: The 'tea estate' definition in s.25 of the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act applied in its 'not less than one hundred acres' form in October 2020, so the answer can state that threshold as the rule.
disagreements.verifier_position: The corpus records that Act No. 20 of 2005 s.10(c) substitutes 'twenty hectares' for 'forty hectares' in that definition and that the substitution could not be applied because the as-enacted baseline reads 'one hundred acres'. The threshold in force at the matter date is therefore unknown from the corpus and is on the face of the 2005 Act twenty hectares, about forty-nine acres, not one hundred acres. The conclusion that a twenty acre property is not a tea estate survives either way, but the rule as stated in the gold answer is probably wrong.

disagreements.researcher_position: No stamp duty authority for a conveyance is in the corpus, because Stamp Duty (Special Provisions) Act s.4 does not list a deed of transfer among the specified instruments and conveyance duty is a provincial levy; the step therefore rests only on Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (6).
disagreements.verifier_position: The rate is indeed outside the corpus, but the Stamp Duty Act, No. 43 of 1982 is in the corpus and s.13 of the 2006 Act expressly keeps it operative for instruments relating to the transfer of immovable property. Section 22(2) of the 1982 Act puts a duty on the attesting notary to take all reasonable steps to satisfy himself that the value on which stamp duty is paid represents the value of the property conveyed, and s.24(b) makes the duty payable by the grantee. Those are steps this notary must take and they were missed.

disagreements.researcher_position: The consent required is that of the Tea and Rubber Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Board.
disagreements.verifier_position: Act No. 20 of 2005 s.3 renamed the Act and the Board to the Tea, Rubber and Coconut Estates (Control of Fragmentation) Act and Board. The corpus edition keeps the 1958 names because the renaming is a body-wide substitution that was recorded as not applied, so the answer's naming is an artefact of the corpus edition rather than the law at the matter date.

Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (14) (corporate seal and board resolution) and rule (17)(b) to (e) (folio extract, certificate of incorporation, photographs) are all post-2020 text; the answer's document-collection steps that echo them are not safely matter-date steps.

missing_definitions_or_exceptions: The proviso to Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (17) allows the parties to dispense with the search in writing; the map states the search duty without it.

Land (Restrictions on Alienation) Act s.4(4)(a) requires the company secretary to report to the Registrar of Lands every six months that foreign shareholding has not reached fifty per cent, and s.2(2)(b) supplies the cure periods where it does. Neither is in the map, and both are things the notary should warn the board about.

Notaries Ordinance s.31 rule (29) (copy and list to the Registrar of Lands of the district where the land lies) is the source for registering in the Bandarawela registry rather than the notary's own district; CL-M062-Q01-023 asserts the Bandarawela registry without it.
Stamp Duty Act s.24(b) (duty payable by the grantee, that is by the purchasing company) and s.6(1) (payable before or at the time of execution) were not added but bear on the same step.
case_law_dependence: None. Nothing in the answer needs a judicial authority, and the validator's case law regex is clean. The customary thirty year title search period, which the researcher deliberately left out and recorded as a corpus gap, is the one point of conveyancing practice with no statutory source; leaving it out is the right call for a statute-only benchmark.
